items.title: Governing the next generation: a framework for the safe and equitable deployment of artificial intelligence, robotics, and immersive technologies in ophthalmology
items.abstract: Objective A new generation of technologies – artificial intelligence (AI), AI-guided surgical robotics, and immersive systems including virtual and augmented reality – are transforming ophthalmic practice across diagnoses, surgery, training, and patient engagement. Each domain has generated compelling clinical evidence; each has also exposed governance gaps – that, if unaddressed, risk entrenching inequalities, undermining patient safety, and erode clinical trust. This Mini Review synthesises the governance landscape across all three technology domains. Methods A narrative review of primary evidence, regulatory frameworks, and governance literature was conducted across AI diagnostics, AI-guided robotic surgery, and immersive technology platforms in ophthalmology, with a focus on publications between 2018 to 2026. Results Five cross-cutting governance failures common to all three domains are identified: dataset underrepresentation in training and validation; the absence of equity surveillance in post-deployment monitoring; an interpretability gap at the point of clinical use; an absent regulatory framework for agentic and continuously learning systems; and a lack of structured AI literacy in clinical training. Conclusion We propose a unified five-domain governance framework applicable across AI, robotics, and immersive technology in ophthalmology. Governance should not be a constraint on innovation – it should form the infrastructure on which innovation can be safely scaled.

items.title: Governing the Public-Sector Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Ghana: Data Sovereignty, Human Accountability and the Limits of Technical Oversight
items.abstract: This article contends that the decisive moment in the governance of public-sector artificial intelligence in Ghana is the moment of acquisition. A system’s deployment, audit, and later challenge all matter, but each is shaped by an earlier and far less visible choice: the tender document, the evaluation criteria, and the contract through which a public institution either retains or quietly surrenders its capacity to answer for the decisions the system will later inform. Ghana entered the final quarter of 2026 with a National Artificial Intelligence Strategy launched by the President on 24 April 2026, a Responsible AI Office announced but not yet shown to be operational, an Emerging Technologies Bill still under stakeholder review, and consultation drafts to replace the Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) and to amend the Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), none of which has been enacted. The binding law governing the State’s acquisition of AI therefore remains the general law: the 1992 Constitution, Act 843, Act 1038, the Electronic Transactions Act, 2008 (Act 772), and the Public Procurement Act, 2003 (Act 663) as amended in 2016 and 2025, now supplemented by the Value for Money Office Act, 2026. Read together, these instruments impose meaningful obligations on public acquirers of AI, chiefly through articles 23 and 296 of the Constitution, the security and processor-contract duties in sections 28 to 31 of Act 843, the incident-reporting and critical information infrastructure regime of Act 1038, and the attribution and retention rules of Act 772. They also contain structural gaps which the procurement process is presently ill-equipped to close, namely a trade-secret limitation on the right to know the logic of automated decisions, an exclusion of decisions authorised by enactment from the automated-decision right, broad exemptions for national security, crime and taxation, and a procurement review system that grants standing to disappointed bidders but not to the citizens whose lives the purchased system will govern. The article develops a principle of non-delegable answerability and an Accountable Acquisition Framework of five conditions, distinguishes throughout between confirmed legal and policy requirements and proposed safeguards, and specifies the evidence that regulators, auditors, courts and researchers would need to evaluate implementation.

items.title: HCXAI-BR: A Reproducible Benchmark for Human-Centered Explainability and Contestability in Brazilian Health Information Guidance
items.abstract: Evaluating lay-facing health guidance from Large Language Models (LLMs) in the Global South requires human-centered explainability (HCXAI) tailored to local health systems and vulnerable populations. We introduce HCXAI-BR, a reproducible evaluation protocol featuring a five-axis, behaviorally anchored rubric—Safety, Accessible Language, Local Contextualization, Contestability, and Transparency—applied to 15 low-risk health scenarios in Brazilian Portuguese. In a pilot model-identity-masked evaluation of six global and national LLMs (90 responses), top-tier global proprietary and adapted commercial models achieved comparable performance (GPT-5.6 Luna 7.33/10, Sabiá-4 BR-SP 7.03/10, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 6.83/10), outperforming the national open-weight models, even on local contextualization within Brazil’s public health network (SUS/UBS). These pilot-scale comparisons, from fifteen prompts and a single response per model, demonstrate the protocol’s ability to discriminate between models, not a statistically validated ranking. An instrument-diagnostic pass resolved conceptual ambiguities between safety directives and epistemic humility, improving contestability inter-rater agreement (κ = 0.485). Our findings demonstrate that post-training alignment of capable base models offers a more viable path toward human-centered, sovereign AI in resource-constrained health ecosystems than small-scale pre-training from scratch. This single, confounded comparison (parameter count and training budget differ between the two models) should be read as a provisional, exploratory observation rather than a general, statistically established claim. SUS and UBS, used above, abbreviate Brazil’s Unified Health System (Sistema Único de Saúde) and its primary-care clinics (Unidades Básicas de Saúde), respectively.

items.title: How AI Dependence Influences Employees' Innovative Work Behavior: The Roles of Challenge-Hindrance Appraisals and Transactional Leadership
items.abstract: The extent to which employees rely on artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a new inflection point for organizational innovation. However, whether this “AI dependency” unleashes innovative potential or implicitly diminishes the willingness to innovate remains a subject of ongoing debate in academia. An analysis of data from 220 full-time employees reveals that AI dependency indirectly promotes innovative work behavior by stimulating challenge stress appraisals; simultaneously, it undermines employees' innovation input by exacerbating the perception of hindrance stressors. The findings offer micro-level evidence for understanding the psychological paradoxes in human-machine collaboration and extend the application boundaries of COR theory and the challenge-hindrance stress framework into the context of human-AI interaction. In practice, this study suggests that to truly unlock the innovation dividends of AI, merely introducing the technology is insufficient; organizations must also critically rethink management logic centered on transactional leadership.

items.title: Impact of a Peer Support Group Intervention on the Quality of Work Life of Medical Residents: A Quasi-experimental Study
items.abstract: Background and objective Medical residency involves substantial academic, clinical, and occupational demands that may affect physicians' well-being and quality of work life (QoWL). Peer support groups (PSGs) may provide structured opportunities for social support and collective reflection within this demanding occupational context. This study aimed to compare global QoWL between resident physicians who participated in a PSG intervention and those in a control group. Materials and methods A non-randomized, two-group quasi-experimental study included 117 resident physicians from a private tertiary-care hospital. Participants were sequentially allocated to an intervention group (n = 61) or to a control group (n = 56). The intervention consisted of six 60-minute weekly PSG sessions conducted in closed groups of 6-10 residents. The primary outcome was the proportion of participants with satisfactory global QoWL, assessed using the short version of the CVT-GOHISALO instrument. Its seven dimensions were evaluated as secondary measures, and mindful attention was assessed as a process-related characteristic using the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS). Between-group comparisons were performed using the Pearson χ² test. Exploratory three-variable contingency tables based on Feinstein's simultaneous-effects framework were used to examine the primary outcome in relation to individual, clinical, occupational, and process-related characteristics. Results Satisfactory global QoWL was observed in 75.4% of the intervention group and 62.5% of the control group, corresponding to an absolute between-group difference of 12.9 percentage points. This difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.131). Among the secondary QoWL measures, the largest absolute between-group difference was observed for safety at work (65.6% vs. 50.0%; p = 0.088), although none of the dimensional comparisons reached statistical significance. Exploratory simultaneous-effects analyses showed heterogeneous intervention-outcome patterns across individual and occupational characteristics. Differences were descriptively larger among women and residents in critical-care services, whereas the pattern was attenuated or absent in some other strata. Workplace violence was associated with lower satisfactory QoWL in both study groups. Conclusions Resident physicians who participated in the PSG intervention showed a numerically higher proportion of satisfactory global QoWL than those in the control group, although the difference did not reach statistical significance. Exploratory analyses indicated that this pattern varied across individual and occupational contexts. PSGs may represent a complementary component of occupational-health strategies for medical residents, but further controlled studies with larger samples are needed to determine whether the observed patterns represent reproducible intervention effects.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Future of Management and Employment
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence also known as AI refers to the creation of computer system and machine that can carry out tasks that normally need thinking. Artificial Intelligence task includes learning, reasoning, problem solving, decision making and innovating ideas. Artificial intelligence is a crucial part of modern business and assist us in various ways – such by analyzing vast amount data, aiding in decision making, formulating strategies and maintaining business records. This study focuses on the impact of advancing Artificial Intelligence system on management during the next decade. Much of the attention around Artificial intelligence and work revolves around the replacement versus augmentation debate. According to previous literature, rather than simply replacing task, machine learning tools can complement human decision making.

items.title: Improving User Experience in AI-Enabled Digital Products through Human-Centered Design
items.abstract: This research proposal explores how Human-Centered Design can improve user experience in AI-enabled digital products, with particular attention to transparency, user control, and calibrated trust. The work draws on existing academic literature and synthesizes findings from previous studies to examine how these factors influence human-AI interaction. It presents the research background, problem statement, objectives, research questions, and a proposed exploratory mixed-methods methodology. The proposal aims to establish a foundation for investigating how transparent AI interactions and meaningful user control can support appropriate user trust and improve overall user experience. This document presents a literature-based research synthesis and a proposed study; it does not report newly collected participant data or completed empirical findings.

items.title: Inclusive Design in Smart Healthcare
items.abstract: This chapter presents a literature review of research at the intersection of inclusive design, healthcare, and smart technologies. The study analyses peer-reviewed publications identified through an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted search and screening process using the keywords “inclusive design”, “healthcare”, and “smart”. The aim is to identify dominant research themes and examine how user groups are represented in this body of literature. The results show that research is concentrated around smart and digital health technologies, healthcare environments, and conceptual design frameworks, with a strong focus on specific user categories such as older adults, people with disabilities, and patients with medical conditions. The findings highlight a tendency towards category-based approaches to inclusion, with limited consideration of broader and more complex forms of user diversity. The chapter contributes to the field by providing a structured overview of current research and by reflecting on the implications of user representation for inclusive design in smart healthcare.

items.title: Influence of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Tools on Teachers' Instructional Delivery in Public Senior Secondary Schools in Port Harcourt Metropolis.
items.abstract: This study investigated the influence of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Tools on Teachers' Instructional Delivery in public senior secondary schools in Port Harcourt Metropolis. Specifically, the study examined the influence of adaptive learning systems, chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading systems, and predictive analytics on teachers' instructional delivery. Three research objectives, three research questions, and three null hypotheses guided the study. A descriptive research design was adopted. The target population comprised 1,866 teachers, from which a sample of 329 respondents was determined using Taro Yamane's formula. The multistage sampling technique was adopted for the sampling of the study. The instrument for data collection was a researcher’s designed questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence-Driven tools on Teachers' Instructional Delivery. The instrument face and content was validated by three experts, one in Measurement and Evaluation and two in Educational Management in Rivers State University. The internal consistency of the instrument was determined using the cronbach Alpha statistics which yielded a reliability coefficient of 0.83. The data collected for the study was analyzed using mean and standard deviation for answer the research questions, while the null hypotheses were tested using independent sample t-test at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that adaptive learning systems, chatbots, automated grading systems and predictive analytics influence teachers’ instructional delivery to a high extent, while intelligent tutoring systems influence teachers’ instructional delivery to a low extent. The hypotheses indicated no significant difference in the mean ratings of teachers in Port Harcourt City Local Government Areas and Obio/Akpor Local Government Areas on teachers’ instructional delivery. Based on the findings, it was recommended among others that; school administrators provide teachers with continuous technical support on adaptive learning systems, and the Rivers State Ministry of Education should formulate clear chatbots policy guidelines and training for effective instructional delivery.

items.title: Innovative digital learning and teaching approaches for developing professional competence in nursing students: a scoping review
items.abstract: Innovative pedagogical approaches have emerged as potential solutions for promoting professional competence in the digital age, as technology integration into nursing education has highlighted the need for such strategies. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on innovative teaching and learning approaches used in nursing education and the professional competence outcomes, barriers, strategies and recommendations reported, with a view to informing future curriculum development. A literature search was conducted on 23 October 2026 in Web of Science, CINAHL, ERIC, PubMed and Scopus, covering articles published from January 2019 to the search date. Search terms were generic rather than technology-specific. Research questions and eligibility criteria were structured using the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. Results were synthesized inductively, reported outcomes were mapped to Miller’s pyramid of clinical competence, distinguishing objective from self-reported measures, and methodological quality was appraised with design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklists. A total of 33 studies were included. Three main themes were identified: (1) Teaching methods, (2) Barriers and challenges of educational technologies and (3) Strategies and recommendations for advancing nursing education. The approaches fell into five categories; all four studies of tools supported by artificial intelligence were published in 2025 or 2026. Objective assessments supported placements at “Knows” in 20 studies, “Knows how” in three and “Shows how” in 17; six studies had no objectively assessed competence outcome. No study reported outcomes at the highest level of Miller’s pyramid (“Does”). Within the studies retrieved, simulation and virtual reality were investigated most often, and objectively assessed gains were reported mainly for performance under controlled conditions; transfer to independent clinical practice was not evaluated. Findings for game-based approaches were mixed, and mobile learning was most often associated with knowledge and observed skill performance. Confidence in the reported benefits is limited by heterogeneous designs, variable methodological quality, reliance on self-report at the “Knows how” level and outcomes measured mostly within two weeks of the interventions. The map is not exhaustive, and comparative, longitudinal evaluations are needed before the relative value of these approaches can be judged.

items.title: Internalising externalities through global technologies: an information systems–based extension of RBV and CBV
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to advance strategic management theory by proposing iRBV – an Information Systems-based extension of the resource-based view (RBV) and capability-based view (CBV). This essay argues that globally available technologies fundamentally change the role of firm resources and capabilities, enabling firms not merely to respond to market conditions but to reshape the rules by which markets operate. Drawing on RBV and CBV, the author proposes iRBV as a framework for understanding how firms can adopt and adapt global technologies – such as artificial intelligence and blockchain – to internalise externalities and create new markets. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a viewpoint on how firms can proactively reshape their environment by incorporating externalities into their strategies. The author proposes iRBV – an information systems (IS)-based extension of the RBV, CBV and natural RBV – as a theoretical advancement that enables management scholars and practitioners to develop business models capable of addressing market externalities, including climate change, at the firm level. Findings Through two illustrative cases – ChatGPT and the Libra coin – this essay demonstrates how global technologies can enable firms to reshape markets and internalise externalities that lie beyond the scope of traditional RBV and CBV. Climate change mitigation is presented as one significant application of this mechanism. Research limitations/implications iRBV is presented as a theoretical provocation rather than a fully operationalised framework. Its primary limitation is the reliance on illustrative cases rather than systematic empirical evidence. Future research should develop the microfoundations of iRBV – specifically the routines, heuristics and higher-order capabilities that enable firms to adopt and adapt globally available technologies for externality internalisation. Additional boundary conditions require investigation, including the applicability of iRBV beyond digital technologies, the role of power asymmetries and path dependencies in capability activation and the conditions under which profit-maximisation logic aligns with – rather than diverges from – the internalisation of societal externalities. Practical implications iRBV equips managers with a theoretical lens for identifying externalities as strategic opportunities rather than regulatory obligations. Firms with strong IS capabilities – such as those already deploying artificial intelligence (AI) or blockchain – are well positioned to develop business models that internalise externalities while generating profit. iRBV encourages managers to incorporate a global view of their strategic environment into firm strategy, treating the internalisation of externalities not as a cost of doing business but as a potential source of market dominance. Social implications iRBV suggests that addressing societal externalities – including climate change – need not depend solely on top-down regulation or international agreements. By providing firms with a profit-driven mechanism for internalising externalities, iRBV enables a bottom-up approach in which individual firms take the lead in reshaping market rules and addressing global challenges. This shifts the locus of responsibility from governments and international bodies to firms themselves, driven by intrinsic strategic logic rather than external mandate. If widely adopted, iRBV could contribute to a broader transformation in how business and society relate to one another in the face of global challenges. Originality/value This paper advances RBV and CBV into iRBV, a theoretical extension that positions globally available technologies as levers for internalising market externalities through intrinsic, profit-driven firm strategies. Illustrative examples demonstrate how technologies such as blockchain and AI could enable firms to address climate change – including CO2 traceability, cryptocurrency-based climate incentives and environmentally-linked search restrictions – while simultaneously achieving market dominance.

items.title: Is it true that Generative AI is Shaping Employee Identity and Working Practices to Become More "Digital"?
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is changing contemporary workplaces by influencing not only task execution but also employees’ understandings of professional competence, roles, and identity. This article explores how employees experience and negotiate changes in work practices and professional identity as GenAI becomes integrated into everyday work. Using an exploratory qualitative and interpretive approach, the study frames GenAI adoption, work-practice transformation, identity negotiation, and human–AI collaboration as interrelated analytical dimensions. The analysis indicates that GenAI can shift work from direct task execution toward task orchestration, in which employees formulate instructions, assess and revise AI outputs, and retain responsibility for final decisions. The resulting identity change is not automatic or uniform: employees may come to view themselves as AI-augmented professionals while also negotiating boundaries around expertise, autonomy, accountability, and meaningful work. GenAI can support efficiency and access to knowledge, yet it may also create dependence, intensified work expectations, and uncertainty about the value of human expertise. The article therefore conceptualizes digital employee identity as a negotiated and potentially hybrid professional identity rather than a simple consequence of technology use. These insights extend discussion of strategic human resource management by highlighting the importance of AI literacy, continuous learning, responsible AI governance, and human-centered work design. The conclusions should be interpreted in light of the exploratory design and the need for further empirical investigation across organizational and occupational contexts.

items.title: Just Because You Can, Does Not Mean You (Always) Should: The Ethical Implications of Using Generative AI in Chemistry Education
items.abstract: The proliferation of accessible generative AI platforms continues to accelerate in society. With this growth, educators are looking to understand how to best train their students to engage in their work and society with this new technology. Most research in this realm has focused on training students to consider when and how to use generative AI, with newer work focused on the impacts on learning. Yet, there has been little exploration of training educators and educational researchers on when and how to use generative AI. While there are some nascent ethical codes emerging, individual exploration of whether, when, and how to use AI in our role as educators deserves attention. In this manuscript, we describe three frameworks of normative ethics, namely, utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics, and explore instructor use cases for generative AI. We do not intend this work to advocate for a specific stance on the use of AI but to invite the reader and our community to engage with the question of their own ethical stance in the context of their own use of the new technology.

items.title: Large-scale clinical application of human-AI collaborative quality improvement program for prenatal ultrasound in an underdeveloped region of China: a quasi-experimental study
items.abstract: To evaluate whether human-AI collaborative models were associated with greater improvements in prenatal ultrasound quality compared with a purely-AI model in an underdeveloped region. We deployed an AI-based quality control system at county-level hospitals in Jiangxi, China, collecting ultrasound images covering 23 planes from mid-to-late trimester prenatal ultrasound screening from January to December 2024. The system scored each image (0-100) and classified it as standard (≥ 80) or non-standard (< 80). Three quality control models—purely-AI, theoretical training alongside AI (T-A), and hybrid human-led alongside AI (H-A)—were allocated at the prefecture-level city (non-randomized). A difference-in-differences framework was used to estimate the associations of the H-A and T-A models compared with the purely-AI group. Parallel trend tests were performed to assess the parallel trends assumption. A total of 131,024 images taken by 192 sonographers across 67 hospitals were collected. All three groups showed significant pre-to-post improvements in both standardisation and missing rates (all P < 0.001). The improvement in standardisation rate was 21.5% (95% CI: 20.7–22.3) for H-A, 19.6% (18.1–21.1) for T-A, and 19.3% (18.4–20.2) for purely-AI. Compared with the purely-AI group, the H-A group was associated with an absolute improvement of 2.2% (95% CI: 1.0–3.4; adjusted OR: 1.53, 95% CI: 1.22–1.93; P < 0.001), whereas the T-A group showed no significant additional benefit: 0.3% (95% CI: −1.4 to 2.0; adjusted OR: 1.14, 95% CI: 0.79–1.66; P = 0.479). In exploratory subgroup analyses, the H-A group showed potential additional benefits in specific subgroups. The H-A model was associated with a modest additional improvement compared with the purely-AI model in this underdeveloped region. These findings suggest that AI-based QC may serve as a foundational component, while the hybrid human-led intervention, though promising, requires further validation in outcome-linked studies.

items.title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
items.abstract: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.

items.title: Learner agency and academic engagement in AI-supported higher education: The roles of e-learning autonomy and self-efficacy
items.abstract: The increasing availability of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to university students raises important questions regarding learners’ responsibility for their work and sustained engagement when assistance is easily accessible. This study investigated the relationships among e-learning autonomy, learning self-efficacy, and academic engagement within an AI-supported higher education environment. A cross-sectional online survey of 223 undergraduate students employed adapted measures to assess perceived capacity for self-directed learning, confidence in personal abilities, and participation in academic activities without excessive dependence on AI assistance. Regression-based mediation analysis indicated that e-learning autonomy was positively associated with both learning self-efficacy and academic engagement. Learning self-efficacy was also positively associated with engagement and showed a significant positive indirect association between autonomy and engagement, alongside a significant direct association. These results highlight autonomy and self-efficacy as interconnected learner resources linked to academic engagement in contexts where AI assistance is present. The findings advance understanding of the human dimensions of AI-supported higher education and underscore the need for institutions to address both AI access and the cultivation of students’ ownership of learning and confidence in their abilities.

items.title: Learning Compact State Abstractions for LLM Agents
items.abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.

items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore how users leverage tools based on large language models (LLMs) to self-manage psychological well-being. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on affordance theory, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 participants and analyzed their use of ChatGPT for psychological well-being using grounded theory techniques. Findings Users learned about ChatGPT's potential through external influences, experimentation, and prior experiences. As their understanding evolved, they actualized various affordances but also encountered barriers when repurposing the tool for psychological well-being. Originality/value This study provides an empirically grounded account of how individuals appropriate a general-purpose LLM for psychological well-being. It identifies context-specific patterns for further affordance research and proposes user-informed design guidelines for LLM-enabled chatbots.

items.title: Linking employee engagement and innovative work behaviour through psychological safety among lecturers in Chinese public universities
items.abstract: Lecturers’ innovative work behaviour is central to the innovative capacity of Chinese public universities. Although employee engagement has been consistently linked to innovative work behaviour, previous studies have examined intrapersonal mediators, such as psychological empowerment and work–life balance, leaving interpersonal risk less clearly understood. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory and Social Exchange Theory, this study examines whether perceived psychological safety statistically mediates the association between employee engagement and innovative work behaviour. Cross-sectional survey data from 384 full-time lecturers at 15 public universities in Shandong Province, China, were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Employee engagement was positively associated with perceived psychological safety and innovative work behaviour, and perceived psychological safety was positively associated with innovative work behaviour. Significant positive direct and indirect associations were consistent with complementary partial statistical mediation. These findings support perceived psychological safety as one potential interpersonal pathway linking engagement and innovative work behaviour, without establishing temporal or causal ordering. Universities may therefore consider supporting both lecturer engagement and conditions conducive to safe idea expression, although the effects of such practices require further evaluation.

items.title: Longitudinal associations among curiosity, Human–AI trust, and functional dependence in generative AI use
items.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into university students’ information seeking and problem solving, individuals’ curiosity, trust in GenAI, and functional dependence on it may interact over the course of continued use. However, the longitudinal relationships among curiosity, Human–AI trust, and functional dependence, as well as their potential transmission mechanisms, remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on information gap theory, a cognitive resource perspective, and the trust and reliance framework in automation, this study adopted a three-wave longitudinal design and a cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) to examine the dynamic relationships among curiosity, Human–AI trust, and functional dependence on GenAI among university students. A total of 952 Chinese university students participated in three waves of data collection at approximately one-year intervals (M age (T3) = 20.35 years). The results showed consistent bidirectional positive cross-lagged associations between Human–AI trust and functional dependence across both time intervals. In contrast, the relationship between curiosity and functional dependence was temporally asymmetric: T1 curiosity positively predicted T2 functional dependence, whereas T2 functional dependence positively predicted T3 curiosity; the corresponding reverse paths were not significant. In addition, two significant longitudinal indirect pathways through functional dependence were identified: T1 Human–AI trust was indirectly associated with T3 curiosity through T2 functional dependence, and T1 curiosity was indirectly associated with T3 Human–AI trust through T2 functional dependence. These findings suggest that functional dependence may serve as an important behavioral pathway linking curiosity and Human–AI trust, and provide longitudinal evidence for understanding how curiosity, trust, and functional dependence interact over time during university students’ continued use of GenAI.

items.title: Mental Health in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: How AI Use Affects Individual Emotion Regulation and Psychological Autonomy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used not only to obtain information or complete tasks, but also to interpret feelings and make sense of difficult experiences. This review considers how such use may relate to emotion regulation and psychological autonomy. Drawing on self-determination theory and process-based accounts of emotion regulation, it examines evidence of both support and risk. Conversational systems may help users name emotions, consider alternative interpretations, and practise coping strategies in settings that feel private and accessible. However, these benefits should not be assumed to persist: when users routinely hand over emotional interpretation or personal decisions to a system, they may have fewer opportunities to exercise their own judgement. The implications therefore depend on the purpose and pattern of use, users' psychological needs and developmental circumstances, and the design of the system. The review discusses implications for AI developers, mental-health practitioners, educators, and policymakers.

items.title: Modeling Event-Conditioned Emotional Expression Response with LLM Agents in a Synthetic Social Simulation
items.abstract: Emotions are central drivers of human behavior, yet most behavioral models fail to capture their role in shaping perception, decision-making, and collective action. Application areas such as emergency response and public health are especially constrained by the lack of emotion-aware modeling. While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into agent-based models (ABMs), little work has examined how to endow LLM agents with emotional reasoning or validated their ability to reproduce empirically observed emotional patterns. This study addresses this gap by introducing a hierarchical prompting framework that conditions LLM agents with demographic, psychological, and contextual cues to generate event-conditioned emotional responses to real-world events. We validate the resulting event-conditioned emotional responses against large-scale social media reaction data derived from the Social Science One Facebook URL Shares Dataset, complemented by demographic and personality benchmarks. Our simulation results reproduce both polarized and consensus-driven emotional patterns with significant fidelity, supporting the application of LLM agents for emotion-aware modeling in behavioral simulations. We also find, however, that systematic gaps in emotional expression of LLM agents and human populations exist, such as the underexpression of anger relative to human baselines. As such, these findings highlight the need for continued calibration if LLM agents are to serve as proxies for human populations in behavioral modeling. By quantifying their divergence from human populations in terms of emotional expression, we hope that our methods can aid in this effort.

items.title: MOTIVATIONAL FACTORS AND THEIR IMPACT ON EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE; LITERATURE REVIEW
items.abstract: Motivation is widely regarded as one of the most important determinants of how well employees perform, yet the research on its sources and effects is spread across several competing theories. This paper reviews the scholarly literature on motivational factors and their impact on employee performance. It first clarifies the key constructs, then examines the major theoretical traditions: content theories (Maslow, Herzberg, McClelland), process theories (expectancy, equity, goal-setting), and self-determination theory. It then synthesizes empirical evidence on the principal motivational factors in organizations: financial rewards, recognition, job design, goals and feedback, fairness, leadership and work environment, and opportunities for growth. The review finds that performance is shaped by the interaction of intrinsic and extrinsic factors rather than by any single driver; that well-designed work and clear, challenging goals have consistently strong support; that financial rewards influence performance but can weaken intrinsic motivation when experienced as controlling; and that the relationship between job satisfaction and performance is real but moderate. Limitations of the evidence and directions for future research are discussed.

items.title: Motivational regulation after an eight-week peer-mentoring programme in Colombian youth swimmers: A pre-post pilot study
items.abstract: Purpose. To estimate regulation-specific pre-post changes after an eight-session peer-mentoring programme in Colombian youth swimmers and assess robustness to missing items, distributional assumptions and participant inclusion. Materials and methods. This single-group pilot study analysed all 29 swimmers aged 10–14 years with paired Sport Motivation Scale (SMS-28) records. Seven four-item regulations were scored on the original 1–7 metric when at least three items were available. Mean changes received bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs; 20,000 resamples), paired t tests and Cohen’s dz. Monte Carlo sign-flip tests (200,000 resamples), Wilcoxon tests, 20% trimmed-mean tests, Holm correction, reliability estimates and inclusion sensitivities assessed robustness. Results. Five of 1,624 item responses were missing (0.31%). Changes were small and imprecise: intrinsic motivation to know +0.27 (95% CI [−0.11, 0.75]; dz = 0.22), intrinsic motivation to accomplish +0.29 (95% CI [−0.27, 0.70]; dz = 0.22), intrinsic motivation to experience stimulation −0.01 (95% CI [−0.26, 0.21]; dz = −0.02), identified regulation −0.10 (95% CI [−0.54, 0.36]; dz = −0.08), introjected regulation +0.26 (95% CI [−0.39, 0.82]; dz = 0.15), external regulation +0.11 (95% CI [−0.47, 0.52]; dz = 0.08), and amotivation +0.28 (95% CI [−0.43, 0.90]; dz = 0.15). All Holm-adjusted primary p values were 1.00. Omitting two paired records changed intrinsic-accomplishment p from .24 (n = 29) to .02 (n = 27). The age-eligible sensitivity was unchanged. Conclusions. The programme coincided with no clear regulation-specific motivational shift. Complete inclusion and theory-consistent scoring reversed the former favourable conclusion, supporting controlled, fidelity-monitored evaluation rather than causal claims.

items.title: National culture, gender, and work values: A comparative study of job expectations in Brazil and Peru
items.abstract: This study examines how national culture and gender shape job expectations in South America by comparing the importance Brazilian and Peruvian participants assign to 25 intrinsic and extrinsic job characteristics. While previous research has examined cultural or gender differences separately, this study evaluates whether gender differences vary across cultural contexts, clarifying the joint influence of culture and gender on work values. Data were collected from 916 Brazilian and Peruvian participants who rated job characteristics on a five-point scale. Mean rankings, MANCOVA/ANCOVA tests, and post hoc comparisons assessed cultural, gender, and interaction effects while controlling for age and employment status. Spearman rank-order correlations evaluated similarity in value hierarchies, and intrinsic–extrinsic composites examined broader motivational patterns. Results revealed significant main effects for both national culture and gender, with culture explaining the largest share of variance. Brazilian participants placed greater importance on intrinsic characteristics such as accomplishment, intellectual stimulation, and development, whereas Peruvian participants emphasized structure, routine, and stability. Female participants consistently rated both intrinsic and extrinsic characteristics as more important than males across most items and showed greater within-group homogeneity in their responses. Importantly, interaction effects indicated that gender differences did not manifest uniformly across countries, supporting the cultural contingency of gender role expectations. This study advances cross-cultural research on work values by jointly examining cultural, gender, and interaction effects within two economically interconnected South American countries. It contributes to Self-Determination Theory and Social Role Theory by demonstrating how motivational orientations vary across cultural environments and gendered socialization processes. The findings have practical implications for recruitment, job design, and talent management strategies, suggesting that organizations operating in South American contexts should tailor their approaches to reflect both cultural context and gender-specific motivational profiles when attracting and retaining talent.

items.title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
items.abstract: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

items.title: Not Whether but What: A Systematic Review of the Locus of Offloading in Generative AI and Higher-Order Thinking
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reduces the effort of learning tasks, but its effect on students’ higher-order thinking may depend on what is offloaded. This pre-registered systematic review synthesized 26 studies (2024–2026), identified from 4729 records, that measured cognitive load and higher-order thinking in the same higher education sample. Across 21 experimental studies, GenAI conditions most often showed lower load (12 studies) and better higher-order outcomes (14 studies). Lower load coincided with poorer thinking in three studies, none of high quality, and in all three the tool was positioned to perform the target thinking. Most outcomes were self-reports or products created using the available tool, and the only study assessing thinking after the tool was withdrawn found a decline. We propose, as a hypothesis, that offloading supports learning when the tool takes over preparatory work but may undermine it when the tool takes over the thinking the task should exercise.

Araştırma, puan sistemleri, şans çarkları, mini oyunlar ve sürpriz kutu mekanikleri gibi oyunlaştırma unsurlarının içsel motivasyon (algılanan keyif, merak) ve dışsal motivasyon (algılanan ekonomik fayda) üzerindeki etkilerini; bu motivasyonel süreçlerin oyunlaştırılmış özellikleri kullanma niyeti ve satın alma niyetiyle ilişkisini ve kaybetme korkusunun (FOMO) bu ilişkilerdeki moderatör rolünü yapısal eşitlik modellemesiyle test etmektedir. Veriler, Türkiye'deki mobil alışveriş uygulamalarında oyunlaştırma etkinliklerine katılmış 223 kullanıcıdan anket yöntemiyle toplanmış; ölçüm modeli doğrulayıcı faktör analizi, yapısal model ise bootstrap destekli SEM ile değerlendirilmiştir. Bulgular, oyunlaştırmanın hem merakı (β = .693) hem de algılanan keyfi (β = .559) anlamlı biçimde artırdığını; ancak içsel motivasyon unsurlarının satın alma niyeti üzerindeki etkisinin sınırlı kaldığını ortaya koymaktadır. Buna karşın, algılanan ekonomik faydanın satın alma niyeti üzerindeki etkisi modeldeki en güçlü ilişki olarak öne çıkmaktadır (β = .701). Kaybetme korkusunun ise öngörülen moderatör etkiyi sergilemediği; bunun yerine satın alma niyeti üzerinde bağımsız bir doğrudan etki oluşturduğu saptanmıştır (β = .144). Bu bulgular, oyunlaştırma tasarımında dışsal teşviklerin ve kıtlık temelli unsurların stratejik önemini desteklemektedir.

items.title: Patient Acceptability of Artificial Intelligence in a DHN Workflow for Hybrid Mental Health Care
items.abstract: Background Digital mental health tools generate growing volumes of active and passive behavioral data, but integrating these data into clinical care and returning them to patients as usable feedback remains a major challenge. Artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models, are able to interpret such data and draft personalized feedback, offering a potentially scalable way to support this work. Whether AI can be adopted for this purpose, however, may depend less on its technical performance than on whether patients trust and accept it. This study examined how former and current patients in mental health service perceive AI involvement in delivering data-report feedback, comparing fully human (no AI), AI-assisted (hybrid), and fully AI-generated formats. Methods Twenty-five adults who had received outpatient mental health treatment viewed six standardized videos representing two clinical scenarios and the three delivery formats. Participants rated each video using a seven-item acceptability scale, compared the formats, and answered open-ended questions. They were not told which formats used AI until after completing the initial ratings. Results Acceptability differed across formats, F(1.20, 28.7) = 21.22, p < .001. Fully human feedback (mean 6.00) and AI-assisted feedback delivered by a human (mean 5.93) received similar ratings, and both were rated more favorably than fully AI-delivered feedback (mean 4.65). Participants were also more comfortable with AI analyzing their data when a human delivered the feedback than with AI both analyzing and delivering it. Overall, 23 of 25 participants preferred a format that retained human involvement after AI use was disclosed. Participants valued AI for producing clear and thorough summaries but wanted a person to explain and discuss the results. Conclusions Patients accepted AI-generated mental health feedback when a human remained involved in reviewing or delivering it. These findings support using AI to assist with data analysis and report preparation rather than replacing the human interaction involved in mental health care. Larger studies should test this approach in routine clinical settings.

items.title: Perceived artificial intelligence job displacement as an occupational health concern: when meaningful work intensifies workaholism and burnout
items.abstract: Background The World Health Organization classifies burnout as an occupational phenomenon, and artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how it arises. Research on AI and worker health has centered on what employees lose once displaced, not their behavior beforehand. We reasoned that the anticipation of being replaced would prompt a defensive form of overwork, and that this overwork may account for the association between anticipated replacement and burnout. Conservation of Resources theory explains why: facing threatened resources, employees invest still more to protect them, until the investment depletes what it should preserve. Methods We surveyed full-time employees in China’s information and communication technology (ICT) industry, where AI has reshaped job content and skills, across two waves, 1 month apart. Perceived AI job displacement, job meaningfulness, and workaholism (Dutch Work Addiction Scale) were measured at Time 1; burnout at Time 2 (emotional exhaustion subscale, Maslach Burnout Inventory–General Survey). Of 531 first-wave respondents, 337 completed both; attrition was related mainly to demographics, and inverse-probability-weighted estimates matched the results. Confirmatory factor analysis supported construct validity; we tested the moderated mediation with hierarchical regression and bootstrapped conditional process analysis (10,000 resamples). Results Perceived AI job displacement was positively associated with burnout (β = 0.54, p < 0.001) and workaholism (β = 0.41, p < 0.001), with a significant indirect path via workaholism (0.09, 95% CI [0.04, 0.13]). Job meaningfulness did not buffer this association; it amplified it (interaction β = 0.14, p < 0.01). The displacement–workaholism association was about twice as strong at high job meaningfulness (b = 0.44, p < 0.001) as at low (b = 0.21, p < 0.01), and the conditional indirect effect on burnout rose from 0.06 (95% CI [0.02, 0.10]) to 0.12 (95% CI [0.06, 0.19]). The index of moderated mediation was significant (0.05, 95% CI [0.01, 0.10]). Conclusion Among these ICT employees, perceived AI job displacement was associated with higher burnout a month later, and workaholism may account for it. The indirect association was strongest where least expected: among employees who found their work most meaningful. Intensified effort warrants scrutiny rather than approval, and workplace health surveillance during digital transformation may consider treating a sudden escalation of overwork as a potential early warning of burnout.

items.title: Perceived Teacher Support and Student Engagement Among Undergraduate Students: A Correlational Study
items.abstract: The present study examined the relationship between perceived teacher support and student engagement at the undergraduate level. Perceived teacher support was conceptualized through four dimensions: emotional support, academic support, autonomy support, and classroom structure, while student engagement comprised behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the study emphasized the role of supportive learning environments in enhancing student motivation and engagement. A quantitative correlational research design was employed. The sample consisted of 300 undergraduate students selected from four universities, including two public and two private universities. Equal representation was ensured across institution type, with 150 students from public and 150 from private universities. Each university contributed 75 students, including 38 males and 37 females. Perceived teacher support was measured by adapting validated open-access instruments, including the Perceived Teacher Support Scale (PTSS), the Foreign Language Teacher Support Scale (FLTSS), and the Questionnaire on Teacher Support Adaptivity (QTSA). Student engagement was measured using the Student Engagement Instrument (SEI). Data were analyzed to examine levels of perceived teacher support and student engagement, differences based on gender and institution type, and the relationship between the two variables. The findings revealed a significant positive relationship between perceived teacher support and student engagement, indicating that supportive teaching practices enhance behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement among undergraduate students. The study highlights the importance of teacher support in fostering meaningful engagement and offers practical implications for improving teaching practices and learning environments in higher education.

items.title: Perceptual Adaptations to Back-Support Exoskeletons: Evidence From Measures of Perceived Exertion, Mental Demand, Discomfort, and Usability
items.abstract: ObjectiveWe examined perceptual adaptations to using back-support exoskeletons during repetitive lifting tasks.BackgroundBack-support exoskeletons are often used to reduce physical demands during repetitive occupational lifting, yet most existing evidence stems from short-term periods of use. It remains unclear whether these effects persist or change with repeated use.MethodTwenty-seven participants were randomly assigned to a passive exoskeleton, active exoskeleton, or no-device control (ND) group. Participants completed four experimental sessions involving symmetric lifting/lowering at six cycles per minute, with 2-min single-task and 1-min dual-task trials, using a load equal to 15% of body mass lifted from ankle to mid-thigh height. Trials were performed as single-task or concurrent 2-back dual-task conditions. Measures included low-back and leg perceived exertion, NASA-TLX mental demand, localized discomfort, usability, and usefulness.ResultsDuring single-task lifting, low-back and leg perceived exertion increased across trials within sessions in the ND group (∼18%), decreased in the passive group (∼36%), and showed smaller decreases in the active group (∼12%). Dual-task difference scores changed little and were similar among groups. Mental demand showed a different pattern, with lower scores in the active group and gradual reductions over trials and sessions in the passive group. Perceived usability and usefulness increased across sessions by up to ∼25%, with no significant differences between devices.ConclusionPerceptual adaptation to exoskeleton use was progressive, multidimensional, and device-dependent, and was more evident for primary-task effort than dual-task cost.ApplicationRepeated-exposure assessments may provide a more accurate understanding of exoskeleton benefits, discomfort, and acceptance during occupational usage.

items.title: Personal Agentic Twin: User-Controlled Memory and Policy-Scoped Representations for Agentic AI
items.abstract: As AI agents increasingly assist people across digital and physical settings, evidence about individuals accumulates through digital interactions and observations of physical-world activities. When multiple agents maintain separate personal contexts, knowledge about the same person can become fragmented, making it difficult to maintain continuity and user control. We argue that personal AI should instead be organized around a shared personal representation under the individual's control. We propose Personal Agentic Twin, a three-plane architecture that connects distributed evidence to an evolving private twin of the individual, from which purpose-specific scoped twins draw personal knowledge to provide assistance and act on the individual's behalf. Authorization and execution controls link the personal knowledge available to each scoped twin with the actions it is allowed to take and the updates it can propose. We illustrate the architecture through representative application scenarios and call for research on the methods and evaluations needed to realize this vision. Personal Agentic Twin offers a foundation for personal AI that extends people's capabilities while preserving their authority over how they are represented and how agents act on their behalf.

items.title: Platforms, Code and Algorithms: Rethinking Adjudication in the Age of Digital Justice
items.abstract: Dispute resolution is being reconstructed on digital foundations. What began as a narrow mechanism for settling e-commerce complaints, Online Dispute Resolution (ODR), now forms part of the machinery of courts and regulators; arbitration clauses are increasingly written into the code of smart contracts; and judges have started relying on artificial intelligence (AI) to search case law, translate judgments and manage dockets. This paper asks how much of the decision-maker’s role can be delegated to a machine without a loss of legitimacy. Drawing on India, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Singapore, China and the United States, it finds that ODR succeeds when embedded in public institutions with binding outcomes, that smart contract arbitration is workable under current law but strains consent and reasoned awards, and that AI cannot lawfully replace the human adjudicator. It proposes a calibrated framework and notes where India’s 2026 draft judicial AI regulations meet or depart from it.

items.title: Pleasure and Meaning: Mapping Profiles of Job-Related Well-Being in the UK
items.abstract: This paper develops a typology of job-related well-being that integrates hedonic and eudaimonic conceptions of a good working life. Drawing on data from the 2024 UK Skills and Employment Survey, we identify four profiles: flourishers (34%), who experience both high levels of pleasure and meaning at work; languishers (10%), who experience neither; hedonists (31%), who report high pleasure but low meaning; and stoics (25%), who report high meaning but low pleasure. We find that languishers fare worst in terms of both job quality and personal outcomes, while the other three profiles exhibit distinct strengths and weaknesses. Hedonists tend to report lower intrinsic job quality but more manageable work demands, whereas stoics report higher levels of skill use and task discretion alongside greater work intensity and job stress. These trade-offs are less evident among flourishers, although they tend to face a significant income penalty after accounting for their skills and task discretion. Taken together, our findings suggest that no single profile enjoys advantages across all dimensions of job quality.

items.title: Policing and intelligence in the AI revolution: institutional adaptation, governance, and democratic resilience
items.abstract: Technological revolutions have repeatedly reshaped crime, political violence, espionage, sabotage, and the institutions responsible for public safety and democratic resilience. Using a structured comparative case approach and an institutional adaptation framework, this paper examines how the Industrial Revolution transformed policing and intelligence institutions and compares these changes with pressures arising from the contemporary Artificial Intelligence (AI) revolution. The analysis considers four dimensions: technological integration, workforce and training, organizational coordination, and governance. The findings identify AI as an institutional stressor and system shock, with technological capabilities and security threats evolving faster than legal, organizational, and oversight frameworks, thereby creating a security vacuum. Police agencies are adopting operational technologies, automation, and AI-supported decision-making, while intelligence agencies increasingly employ data fusion, signals intelligence, behavioural modelling, open-source intelligence, quantum computing, and international coordination. Meanwhile, cybercrime, terrorism, foreign interference, espionage, organized crime, and digitally mediated political violence increasingly transcend national borders. The paper concludes that institutional resilience depends not only on technological capacity but also on adaptable legal frameworks, workforce development, inter-agency coordination, and democratic oversight that preserve public trust, accountability, privacy, and the rule of law.

items.title: Preparing Future Nurses For An AI-Enhanced Healthcare Environment Through AI Literacy Education
items.abstract: BackgroundWithin the scholarly literature, nurse leaders and nurse educators discuss the need for the profession to embrace Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications. As AI utilization begins to grow, the nursing profession remains slower to adopt, and several educators call for the inclusion of AI literacy in the nursing student curriculum and continued life-long learning for professionals. ObjectivesThe goal of this study was to evaluate undergraduate student nursing knowledge and use of AI applications while providing AI digital literacy instruction that discussed a broad overview of what AI is, ethical and legal considerations of using AI tools in healthcare, discussion of unique and successful approaches to using AI in healthcare, and include practice-based learning to explore free and Library subscription resources that incorporate AI use to refine research questions and search the literature for relevant source materials. MethodsBefore engaging in the study, the study design received IRB exemption as program improvement. Undergraduate nursing students enrolled in the 4351 Consumer of Research course over Fall 2024 and Spring 2025 received the 1.5-hour training and were asked to take pre- and post-surveys to gauge their knowledge and interest in AI. The survey was administered via a Qualtrics platform and QR access code; 9 of the questions were sliding scale questions from 1 -10 and were created by this study’s authors, and the remaining 17 questions were multiple-choice and were part of a validated instrument. Permissions from the original survey author to re-use the instrument were sought and granted. Student responses were gathered voluntarily and anonymously. The 1.5 hour training session covered topics such as how AI is being used in healthcare currently, ethical considerations, patient advocacy, and potential uses for nurses in the clinical setting. Free AI literature tools were demonstrated such as Illicit and SciSpace as well as newly acquired subscription tools such as ScopusAI. Students were encouraged to utilize ChatGPT to develop and refine their research question in the PICO framework. In addition to utilizing AI literature tools, students were taught how to effectively search Pubmed Medline and EBSCO’s CINAHL database using advanced search techniques and controlled vocabulary. ResultsThe pre-survey garnered 94 responses, and the post-survey garnered 16 responses. Results were analyzed using the Qualtrics Results tool. In the pre-survey, most participants mentioned unfamiliarity with AI literature research tools such as Elicit, ScopusAI, SciSpace, and others. In terms of frequency of access, the majority of the participants stated that they rarely to slightly use AI tools. Many of the participants were aware of ChatGPT and some participants mentioned other tools such as Sherpath AI, snapchatAI, and google searching AI functionality that they were familiar with.

items.title: Psychological pathways to sustainable employee performance: the roles of digital leadership, psychological empowerment, work engagement, and organizational trust
items.abstract: The digital transformation of organizations has intensified interest in the psychological factors associated with employees’ ability to sustain effective performance over time. However, limited research has examined the relationships between digital leadership, psychological empowerment, organizational trust, work engagement, and sustainable employee performance within an integrated framework. Drawing on Social Exchange Theory and the Job Demands–Resources model, this study examines these relationships in digitally transforming organizations in China. Survey data were collected from 550 employees and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results supported all seven hypotheses. Digital leadership was positively associated with psychological empowerment and organizational trust, while psychological empowerment and organizational trust were positively associated with work engagement. Work engagement was also positively associated with sustainable employee performance. The mediation analyses indicated significant indirect relationships between digital leadership and sustainable employee performance through work engagement and through the sequential pathway involving psychological empowerment and work engagement. These findings highlight the relevance of psychological resources and motivational states in understanding sustainable employee performance in digitally transforming workplaces. The study contributes to research on digital leadership by integrating empowerment, trust, and engagement within a framework grounded in Social Exchange Theory and the Job Demands–Resources model. For practitioners, the findings suggest that leadership practices supporting employee autonomy, trust, and engagement may be relevant to maintaining effective performance over time. Given the cross-sectional design, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of associations rather than causal effects.

items.title: Psychological resilience, emotional regulation, and performance pressure in Formula One: A documentary thematic analysis of public driver narratives
items.abstract: Formula One (F1) represents one of the most psychologically demanding environments in elite sport, requiring athletes to perform under conditions of extreme cognitive workload, physiological strain, public scrutiny, and competitive uncertainty. Despite growing recognition of athlete mental health and well-being, limited research has explored how Formula One drivers themselves construct and interpret experiences of performance pressure, emotional regulation, resilience, and identity across their careers. This study employed a documentary, media-based Reflexive Thematic Analysis, informed by a critical realist epistemology, to examine how elite Formula One drivers publicly construct experiences of performance pressure, emotional regulation, resilience, and identity. Data were drawn from publicly available press conference transcripts, podcasts, and published interviews involving 14 current and former Formula One drivers. Analysis was guided by contemporary frameworks of psychological resilience, athletic identity, and transactional stress appraisal. Four interrelated themes were generated: (1) The Dualism of Perfectionism and Self-Blame, (2) Preternatural Equanimity and Functional Appraisal, (3) Narrative Identity and Career Reconstruction, (4) The Interplay of Cognitive Control, Adversity, and Mental Toughness. Findings suggest that, as publicly narrated, resilience in Formula One is not presented as a fixed personality trait but as a dynamic process shaped by cognitive appraisal, emotional regulation, social support, and identity development. These findings provide an account of how drivers construct and communicate psychological adaptation for public audiences, rather than direct evidence of their underlying psychological states. The study contributes to the emerging literature on athlete mental health by providing insight into how psychological adaptation is publicly represented and communicated within one of the world's most demanding sporting contexts. Implications for sport psychology practice, athlete welfare, and integrated mental health support systems in elite motorsport are discussed.

items.title: Psychotherapy 2035: Generative Ai Scenarios Psychotherapy 2035: A Technology Assessment Review of Generative AI Scenarios for Mental Health Care
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is entering psychotherapy faster than evidence, professional norms and regulation can follow, the configuration described by the Collingridge dilemma. This technology assessment review combines a narrative synthesis of PubMed and web searches (9 October 2026) with explorative scenario construction along two axes, locus of delivery and governance regime. Efficacy effects are small, short-lived and heterogeneous; blended and certified formats are better supported than stand-alone chatbots. Documented harms, including inadequate crisis responses, dependence and distress after model updates, concentrate outside clinical settings, and regulation is fragmented. Four scenarios result for 2035: augmented clinician, stepped hybrid care, consumer-companion market and regulated digital therapeutics. They will probably coexist. Governance should prioritize measures that are robust across scenarios (outcome and incident registries, crisis-escalation standards, continuity duties, protected human roles) and monitor early signposts.

items.title: Recursive Collective Intelligence: Emergence on an Equal-Budget Ladder in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly work as teams of agents, and a team is expected to solve problems beyond the reach of any single member. Most evaluations credit a team for outperforming a single agent, without accounting for the additional computation: a team may consume many times the tokens of one agent, and a plain vote over independent answers already explains most of the reported gain. Two questions therefore remain open: When does interaction itself make a group smarter, and can a group improve its next generation by learning from its own work? We answer both with the equal-budget ladder, which grades a group against independent agents at three levels: outperforming a single agent, a compute-matched majority vote, and compute-matched pass@n. On this ladder we define Recursive Collective Intelligence (RCI) as a group whose own output, without a teacher or external labels, makes its next generation smarter at equal cost. Three findings follow. First, interaction improves collective intelligence when it moves information across agents: forwarding split facts lifts groups above pass@n at three model scales, by about a third at 27B. Second, organization emerges spontaneously: identical 27B agents form hubs and improve accuracy by 18 percentage points; encoding their organization in a prompt enables them to reach level 3 at less than half the token budget in a descriptive comparison. Third, groups recursively improve themselves: Two label-free generations progressively climb the ladder, the second 9B generation surpassing both pass@$n$ and a control trained on base-model turns; on PlanBench, HiddenBench and Hanabi, each generation outperforms its predecessor on unseen problems for four to six generations. A group therefore outperforms its members when it forwards useful information more efficiently than it spends tokens on coordination, and learns to do so from its own work.

items.title: Recursive entanglement drift: Arbitration shift as a candidate mechanism of relational-epistemic risk in human–AI interaction
items.abstract: Recent work on harmful human–AI interaction has moved from anecdotal reports towards measurement, including research showing how AI sycophancy can produce erroneous beliefs even in idealized rational users. Much of this work focuses on what users believe and what models reinforce, while less is known about how users settle conflicts when an AI-mediated interpretation and an outside source disagree. This paper proposes Recursive Entanglement Drift (RED), a longitudinal framework for relational-epistemic risk in human–AI interaction that describes how recursive exchanges may form a sealed dyad, where outside correction remains present but loses influence. AI outputs can shape subsequent user inputs, which then shape later AI responses. RED's proposed core mechanism is arbitration shift, a change over time toward the AI-mediated frame in epistemic arbitration, the process by which users resolve conflicts between previously AI-mediated commitments and sources outside the human–AI dyad. Source-conflict episodes can document how individual disagreements resolve, while arbitration shift is inferred across episodes within the same user. The paper includes a codebook designed to complement existing transcript-coding systems. Its potential explanatory value beyond trust, dependence, and general belief-revision tendencies remains to be empirically tested. Users may rely heavily on AI while outside sources still influence how conflicts resolve, and the shift may appear with limited emotional or functional reliance on AI. Arbitration shift is predicted to precede stable resistance to correction. If supported, it may provide an early marker of risk not defined by belief content or accuracy; if unsupported, the construct should be revised or rejected.
