items.title: Risk of Bias Assessment Tools for Evidence Synthesis: Evolution, Comparison, and Future Directions in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: A risk-of-bias assessment judges whether flaws in the design, conduct, or analysis of a study could have distorted its effect estimate. Appraisal tools for this task have multiplied, and large language models, a form of artificial intelligence, are now being tested as assessors. This narrative review covers 59 tools for appraising the risk of bias or methodological quality of studies (1981–2026) identified from earlier overviews or organizational resources supplemented by PubMed searches for new tools. This review traces over time three overlapping lines of development: summed scores, structured checklists, and domain-based tools to assess studies against an ideal trial. It compares the seven tools currently recommended for the main study designs, examines their use in traditional Chinese medicine and other complex interventions, and appraises published evidence on assessments using large language models. Domain-based tools pose a clearer causal question than earlier tools but are harder to apply consistently. In reliability studies, chance-corrected agreement between independent assessors was low for the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2; Fleiss' κ 0.16, 95% confidence interval 0.08–0.24) and for the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tool (ROBINS-I; κ 0.06, 95% confidence interval 0.001–0.12). Surveys of reviews show that tools are often poorly chosen and their results unused. Moreover, in traditional Chinese medicine trials, sham acupuncture is not physiologically inert, acupuncturists cannot be blinded, and syndrome-based tailoring is part of the intended intervention only when specified by the protocol; therefore, reviewers must check protocols and registrations. These features call for judgment when RoB 2 is applied, rather than an automatic high-risk rating. Finally, published evaluations of language models differ in terms of models, prompts, tools, samples, reference standards, and metrics; therefore, their results cannot be compared directly. Overall agreement with human judgments on RoB 2 was found to be low to moderate (κ 0.06 to 0.51), and the models are not yet suitable as stand-alone assessors. Here, we propose a conceptual human-in-the-loop workflow in which software retrieves and anchors evidence, trained reviewers make every judgment, and any use of artificial intelligence is fully reported. This approach requires prospective testing of accuracy, agreement, override rates, and total person-time. Priorities for tool development include application guidance for RoB 2 in traditional medicine trials, tested for consistency among assessors; a bias module for trials of artificial intelligence interventions; open benchmark datasets; and signaling questions at the design stage. items.title: SafeCalib: benchmarking security-critical refusal calibration in instruction-tuned language models
items.abstract: Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as gatekeepers for security-sensitive and dual-use requests, yet most AI safety evaluations report refusal as a binary outcome. This leaves a deployment-critical question underexamined: whether a model separates harmful requests from legitimate security work reliably, and whether that separation survives adversarial framing. We introduce a refusal-evaluation framework comprising a two-sided, intensity-stratified error measure—Calibration-Adapted Expected Calibration Error (CA-ECE)—paired Overrefusal/Underrefusal Rate (ORR/URR) measurement, and Adversarial Calibration Shift (ACS), a statistic for how far underrefusal erodes as adversarial prompt framing intensifies. We state its scope explicitly: a refusal decision carries no confidence score, so CA-ECE is not a probability-calibration error but the fixed-weight average $$\tfrac{1}{2}(\bar{\textrm{URR}}+\bar{\textrm{ORR}})$$, whose neutral value 0.5 is shared by any policy that always refuses or never refuses. We instantiate the framework with SafeCalibBench, a 6,080-prompt benchmark covering malware generation, phishing, social engineering, network exploitation and chemical/biological misuse, with binary refusal labels, five adversarial intensity levels and legitimate-security-research hard negatives. Evaluating four instruction-tuned LLMs and three base counterparts on a stratified 2,000-prompt subsample, with intervals from a base-prompt-level cluster bootstrap, we find a consistent tradeoff: instruction tuning reduces direct underrefusal by 58.9 percentage points on average relative to base models but raises overrefusal by 20.0 points (mean ORR $$=24.6\%$$). Base-model CA-ECE (0.506–0.518) lies within 0.02 of the content-independent baseline of 0.5, so their low overrefusal reflects indiscriminate acceptance; instruction-tuned models reach 0.336–0.443. Continuation framing raises underrefusal by up to 37.7 points relative to direct prompts, and refusal behaviour differs significantly across security domains ($$p<0.01$$). All estimates carry a signed, asymmetric classifier bias that we characterise rather than assume away. SafeCalib reframes refusal evaluation from whether a model refused to how far its refusals separate harmful from legitimate use.

items.title: Seeing Through the Lens: Divergent Thinking and the Evaluation of Creative Product Designs
items.abstract: Evaluations of creative products reflect both product characteristics and evaluator attributes. It remains unclear whether the ability to generate original ideas shapes how people evaluate creative products made by others. In this preregistered study, 97 university students first completed the Gough Creative Personality Scale, the openness items of the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and a self-report item on cultural orientation. In random order, they then rated five iconic chair designs on the Creative Product Semantic Scale and completed an Alternative Uses Task with six everyday objects. The chair ratings yielded each chair's perceived originality and perceived functional quality, and a large language model scored the originality of the Alternative Uses Task responses. Divergent-thinking originality did not predict the evaluation of any chair after correction for multiple comparisons, and creative personality did not strengthen this association as predicted. Openness to experience was associated with more favorable ratings of all chairs, whereas cultural orientation, gender, hobbies, and study year were not. In exploratory analyses, the association between perceived originality and perceived functional quality varied across the five chairs. It was strongest for chairs of intermediate perceived originality, a pattern consistent with the most-advanced-yet-acceptable principle. Design features were not manipulated, so this pattern requires confirmation with larger, systematically varied sets of products. Overall, originality in idea generation was not associated with more favorable evaluations of creative products. Evaluator openness and the specific design were more closely related to these judgments.

items.title: ShellBench: What Matters More for AI Agents, Models, or Harness for Everyday Tasks
items.abstract: The use of AI agents among the general public has been increasing exponentially throughout 2026, though it is often hard for users to determine which configuration is most effective for their personal use. To help provide clarity here we introduce ShellBench, 100 day-to-day tasks based on more than 10 million user requests, each set in a realistic workspace with messy files and competing data sources, and graded for both correctness and safety. We evaluate 12 models across 5 agent harnesses at 3 reasoning levels for a total of 53,100 rollouts, 20% of which are on tasks designated for public release. We find that model choice impacts performance more than harness choice, but the three leading models differ by only 1.1 percentage points. GPT-6.1 Sol passed 61.4% of attempts at about one-sixth of GPT-6 Astra's estimated token cost per attempt, while GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%. We also found that harness choice had little effect on either performance or safety with all harnesses scoring between 42.9 (Claude Code) and 45.2 (OpenClaw) for pass@1.

items.title: Short-Term Efficiency, Long-Term Cognitive Cost? A Systematic Literature Review of Large Language Model Use in Professional Work
items.abstract: Many professionals now use large language models (LLMs) at work, and experiments show that the tools make many tasksfaster and improve the immediate output. The worry is that these gains may cost workers some of the skill, judgement and self-knowledgethey would otherwise build or keep. We systematically reviewed empirical research on the cognitive and performance consequences ofLLM use among workers and professionals, published between January 2020 and November 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines,we identified 1,559 records in OpenAlex and Europe PMC and five further studies through citation searching. After screening, 157 studiesremained. Two-thirds were published in 2026, and most come from software development, healthcare and general knowledge work.Randomised and field experiments consistently report short-term gains in speed, output and quality, typically largest for less experiencedworkers. These gains are task-dependent, and LLM-assisted professionals frequently fail to match the model working alone. Fewer than tenstudies measured unaided performance, memory or skill after LLM use. Those that did reported reduced recall of AI-assisted work,impaired skill formation and fragility when access was disrupted. Cross-sectional studies link reliance and confidence in AI with lowerself-reported critical thinking and professional self-efficacy, but self-reported capability loss did not track objective performance.Experience, task fit, mode of use, AI literacy and verification behaviour emerged as moderators. We conclude that the short-term efficiencygain is well supported, while the long-term cognitive cost remains plausible but largely untested in professional settings. We propose aframework and research agenda centred on longitudinal and withdrawal-based designs.

items.title: Single camera computer vision to estimate trunk angles during dynamic manual materials handling work
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine how video capture angle, computer vision platform, and movement pace influence trunk and shoulder angle estimates during manual materials handling (MMH) tasks relative to a multi-camera motion capture system. BACKGROUND: Posture assessment is important for evaluating musculoskeletal disorder (MSD) hazards during MMH work, yet limited guidance exists on how to optimally implement emerging computer vision technologies to inform posture assessment. METHODS: Forty participants performed three common MMH tasks. Video data from eight cameras positioned around the participant were processed using Theia3D to generate criterion trunk inclination and shoulder elevation angles. Individual camera views were also processed through four commercially available single-camera computer vision platforms. Mean absolute differences (MADs) between multi-camera and single-camera angle estimates were calculated. RESULTS: Camera viewing angle had a larger effect on MAD than computer vision platform. Recording lifting, palletizing, or pushing/pulling from directly in front of or behind the participant performed worst (e.g., MAD>20°), regardless of computer vision platform. However, the optimal camera viewing angle (e.g., perspective that limited MAD to ≈5°, or less) was dependent on the computer vision platform used. CONCLUSION/APPLICATION: Computer vision platforms produced consistent differences for all evaluated segments when the camera views captured MMH work from their optimal viewing angle. Users should avoid recording MMH work from anterior or posterior views.

items.title: Stakeholder Acceptance, Trust, and Implementation of AI in Oncology: Mixed Methods Systematic Review
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: AI is entering oncology workflows faster than evidence on stakeholder acceptance, trust, and sustained use. Existing syntheses rarely distinguish anticipated attitudes from actual use across oncology stakeholders. OBJECTIVE: The aim of the study is to synthesize primary empirical evidence on stakeholder acceptance, trust, and implementation of AI in oncology and examine variation by stakeholder group, clinical task, AI exposure, and implementation maturity. METHODS: We conducted a Joanna Briggs Institute-guided mixed methods systematic review with convergent integrated synthesis; the protocol was registered before formal eligibility screening. Eight databases were searched without date or language limits (August 6-9, 2026), yielding 46,206 records and 31,802 unique records. Title and abstract screening used 2 balanced primary allocations, joint bidirectional readjudication, and blinded verification of a stratified 10% (n=3182) sample. Full-text assessment, extraction, and critical appraisal were dual independent. Acceptance/Trust modes and F1-F8 coverage were independently coded across 309 studies and reconciled. Eight integrated findings were anchored to the nonadoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread, and sustainability framework; an emergent economic finding was reported separately. Adjusted stage models controlled for study design, publication format, and publication period; robustness analyses examined screening provenance and appraisal sensitivity. RESULTS: We included 309 primary empirical studies; 187 (60.5%) were published in 2025 or 2026. Exposure ranged from hypothetical opinion to real-world implementation (n=82 studies), but only 6 described routine use. Acceptance was empirically assessed in 267 studies and Trust in 127. Relative to anticipatory stage 1, Acceptance assessment was less frequent in evaluated-interaction stage 2 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.07, 95% CI 0.02-0.25; P<.001) and stages 3+4 (aOR 0.12, 95% CI 0.03-0.45; P=.001). Transparency/explainability coverage (F3) was lower in stages 3+4 (aOR 0.20, 95% CI 0.08-0.47; q<0.001). Workflow/interoperability coverage (F5) was higher and governance coverage (F7) lower in both later contrasts after false discovery rate correction. Trust declined descriptively across stages, but adjusted contrasts were nonsignificant. Eight integrated findings spanned clinical value, performance, transparency, oversight, workflow, readiness, governance, and implementation, plus an emergent stage 1 economic finding. The principal Acceptance, F3, F5, and F7 findings persisted in the 229-study original screening subset. CONCLUSIONS: In oncology, the AI evidence profile appears to differ from anticipated use to implementation. Acceptance was empirically assessed most often before deployment; later-stage studies more often examined workflow and less often examined transparency and governance. The challenge is whether favorable attitudes and early deployment translate into calibrated, governed, and sustained routine use. An interpretive stage-specific model identifies assessment priorities across exposure and implementation contexts, but is not a validated causal or predictive model. Later-stage evaluations should retain measurement of Acceptance, trust calibration, governance, durability, and workflow outcomes. items.title: Strategic leadership in AI-assisted banking decisions: a conceptual framework for critical evaluation and accountability
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly informs strategic banking decisions, yet the presence of human reviewers does not establish that critical evaluation influences organisational commitment. This article examines how strategic leadership can organise the assessment, challenge, and authorisation of AI-assisted strategic recommendations. Drawing on a targeted, non-exhaustive synthesis of research on strategic leadership, human–AI delegation, employee voice, accountability, and AI governance, it develops a conceptual framework centred on the strategic decision episode. The framework connects three processes: independent assessment, consequential challenge, and reasoned commitment. It distinguishes the expression of a material objection from the substantive response it receives and the incorporation of that response into the grounds for authorisation. Six propositions propose how model opacity, verification resources, sponsor control, prospective justification, and independent assessments supplied to approvers shape these connections, while decision uncertainty, irreversibility, and resolution criteria condition the proposed process. The framework identifies objection–response–commitment traceability as an intermediate process outcome, while distinguishing documented connections from substantive reasoning and realised performance. Its contribution is to specify where critical evaluation may lose organisational influence as AI-generated advice moves towards commitment. For banking leaders, it offers a basis for organising responses to material concerns without assuming that additional review necessarily improves decisions. The framework remains untested and provides an agenda for examining both the benefits and costs of alternative evaluation arrangements.

items.title: StreamCoach: Proactive Sports Coaching via Continuous Visual Reasoning
items.abstract: In fitness and sports training, timely action quality assessment (AQA) is essential for learners to identify and correct technical errors during movement execution. However, most AQA methods assess completed performances, limiting their ability to provide timely feedback. Streaming methods alleviate this latency, but limited reasoning hinders their use of subtle movement cues and sport-specific knowledge. Moreover, their fragmented feedback focuses on one body part at a time, overlooking movement details of other body parts and transitions between action phases. To address these limitations, we propose StreamCoach, a streaming AQA framework under the OnCueCoaching paradigm that couples continuous chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with proactive, evidence-gated coaching. Technique-Aware Reasoning tracks body-part movements and action-phase transitions against sport-specific criteria, while Holistic Coaching integrates accumulated evidence to deliver timely, comprehensive feedback on strengths and technical errors. To support training and benchmarking, we construct EE4D-Stream from 1,213 sports video sequences in Ego-Exo4D through LLM-assisted reannotation and manual review of selected claims, pairing dense CoT annotations with evidence-gated speech content. Building on this dataset, we train StreamCoach using Temporal-Semantic Alignment Reinforcement Learning to jointly optimize feedback timing and content. We benchmark 11 offline and streaming baselines on EE4D-Stream, including three proprietary models. StreamCoach achieves state-of-the-art results across intervention timing, action assessment, and coaching quality, surpassing both GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5.

items.title: Student Perceptions, Trust and Willingness to Use Artificial Intelligence for Career Guidance in Higher Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in career counselling, yet limited questionnaire-based evidence exists on how students perceive and accept it. This study examines students' awareness and experience of AI-based career guidance, its perceived usefulness, trust, ethical and privacy concerns, and willingness to use it. A descriptive, quantitative design was adopted. Data were collected through a structured Google Form from 206 undergraduate and postgraduate students of JG University, Ahmedabad, selected by convenience sampling. All five constructs showed high internal consistency . Prior use of digital or online career-guidance services was reported by of respondents, and had used an AI tool or chatbot for career information. Mean scores for usefulness, trust, ethical concerns, and willingness to use were all above the neutral value of 3 on a five-point scale, mostly between 3.6 and 3.9. Protection of personal information was ranked the most important selection factor. A chi-square test showed a significant but modest association between gender and previous use of digital career-guidance services , with more female than male respondents reporting prior use. Multiple regression showed that perceived usefulness, trust, ethical concerns, and importance of features together explained 75.8% of the variance in willingness to use AI career guidance . Ethical, fairness and privacy concerns were the strongest predictor (β = 0.323), followed by importance of features , trust , and usefulness . The findings suggest that acceptance depends on privacy protection, transparency, and fairness as much as on usefulness. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; career guidance; higher education; student perception; trust and transparency; ethical and privacy concerns; willingness to use; multiple regression

items.title: Students’ Perceptions of AI-Assisted Project-Based Learning for Computational Thinking, Creativity, and Algorithmic Thinking in a Logic and Algorithms Course
items.abstract: Purpose – This study examines students’ self-reported levels and perceptions of computational thinking, creativity, algorithmic thinking, and artificial intelligence (AI) in an AI-assisted project-based learning (PjBL) approach implemented in a Logic and Algorithms course. Design/methodology/approach – A quantitative descriptive approach was employed with 42 first-semester undergraduate students participating in 16 learning sessions during one semester. Students completed individual algorithmic projects with access to generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, according to their learning needs. Data were collected after project completion using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire initially consisting of 20 items, of which 18 items were retained for the final analysis following item-level validity evaluation. Findings – The results showed positive self-reported levels across all four constructs. The mean scores were 3.67 (SD = 0.54) for computational thinking, 3.63 (SD = 0.68) for creativity, 3.68 (SD = 0.52) for algorithmic thinking, and 3.97 (SD = 0.57) for AI perception. All four construct scores were significantly higher than the neutral benchmark of 3.00 (p < .001), with large effect sizes. Research limitations – The study used a one-group posttest design with a relatively small sample from a single Logic and Algorithms course, and the data were based on students’ self-reported perceptions. Therefore, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of causal effects or actual learning gains. Platform preference, fre​quency, and intensity of AI use were not quantitatively analysed. Practical implications: AI-assisted PjBL can provide a flexible environment for exploring and developing solutions to algorithmic problems. Its implementation should be accompanied by lecturer scaffolding, verification and modification of AI-generated outputs, documentation of AI use, and learning activities that encourage original ideas and formal algorithmic representations. Originality/value: This study provides a descriptive account of students’ self-reported computational thinking, creativity, algorithmic thinking, and AI perceptions within an introductory Logic and Algorithms course using AI-assisted PjBL. By examining these dimensions simultaneously, the study highlights the distinction between positive perceptions of AI-supported exploratory problem solving and the need to maintain students’ responsibility for originality, verification, and formal algorithmic reasoning.

items.title: Supervision Consultation as an Organizational Resource to Buffer Occupational Burnout: Proposal of a Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background Occupational burnout is a widespread challenge in contemporary workplaces and is associated with reduced employee well-being, productivity, and organizational sustainability. Although resource-based models emphasize the protective role of personal and job resources, organizational-level interventions targeting burnout remain underexamined. Professional supervision represents a potentially scalable organizational resource that may buffer burnout through the enhancement of personal resources such as occupational self-efficacy, work engagement, and job satisfaction. Objective The objective of this research proposal is to describe a planned study evaluating whether sustained supervision consultation—delivered face-to-face or online—may buffer occupational burnout indirectly by strengthening key personal resources across diverse occupational groups. Methods This research proposal describes a planned longitudinal randomized controlled trial with three parallel arms: (1) face-to-face supervision consultation, (2) online supervision consultation, and (3) a waitlist control condition. Structural equation modeling using random-intercept cross-lagged panel models will be used to examine mediation processes over time. Approximately 300 participants from multiple occupational sectors will be recruited. Assessments will be conducted at baseline (T1), 3 months (T2), and 6 months (T3). The proposed intervention consists of 12 biweekly 90-minute group supervision consultation sessions delivered over a 6-month period. Burnout will be measured primarily using the Burnout Assessment Tool (BAT) and supplemented with the Link Burnout Questionnaire (LBQ) to enable comparison across competing conceptualizations. Occupational self-efficacy, work engagement, and job satisfaction will be examined as mediating personal resources. Data will be analyzed using longitudinal structural equation modeling, including mediation and multigroup analyses. Results As of February 2026, the study protocol has been finalized, but participant recruitment and data collection had not yet commenced. Preparatory work was supported by an internal seed grant awarded in June 2021 under the University of Gdańsk UGrants-first Programme. No data analysis had been conducted. The proposed study remains in the planning stage and will be implemented following ethics approval, trial registration, and acquisition of the necessary resources. Findings from the completed study will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications. Conclusions This research proposal describes a planned study evaluating supervision consultation as a preventive organizational intervention for burnout. The study aims to contribute to theory-driven, resource-based approaches to occupational well-being and to inform the development of future organizational interventions.

items.title: Supporting, not replacing: counsellors’ and service coordinators’ perspectives on the use of artificial intelligence in youth online chat counselling
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored to support youth online chat counselling services (OCCS). Understanding stakeholders’ perspectives is essential to guide its effective implementation. This study explored counsellors’ and service coordinators’ perspectives on the role of AI in youth online chat counselling. Methods Sixty-two semi-structured interviews were conducted with counsellors and service coordinators from 33 non-profit OCCS across Belgium, Finland, Hungary, and Spain. Interviews were recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English, and analysed using qualitative thematic analysis in NVivo. Results Four key themes emerged during interviews: (1) attitudes towards AI, (2) current and (3) future applications, and (4) requirements for responsible implementation. Participants opposed AI replacing human counsellors but considered its growing role as inevitable. 6 out of 33 (18.2%) OCCS reported having incorporated a chatbot (at the time of the interview, type not specified). Participant reported current use of AI in OCCS included automated responses, suicide risk identification, and data management functions. Proposed future uses comprised intelligent routing, multilingual support, transcription, resource and referral identification, counsellor training, real-time suggestions and feedback, and documentation and reporting support. Participants emphasised the need for an AI ethical framework that included transparency and continuous human supervision. Discussion Participants viewed AI as a tool to support rather than replace human counsellors, particularly for administrative and service-delivery tasks. Although concerns remained regarding AI's limitations and potential impact on employment, participants identified opportunities for its use, provided AI is used ethically and responsibly. Future implementation of AI in OCCS should be guided by clear task boundaries, robust ethical safeguards, and the active involvement of counsellors and service coordinators throughout the implementation process.

items.title: The Challenges Facing Young Workers in an Ageing Society — Does AI Really Help
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence may reshape the effects of population aging on young workers' productivity and human-capital accumulation. Moving beyond the traditional view that aging primarily affects economic growth through labour-supply reductions, the paper considers the possibility that demographic change also weakens cross-age knowledge transmission and workplace learning. Drawing on Mincer's human-capital theory and on an adapted version of Acemoglu and Restrepo's task-based framework, the study conducts a theory-guided qualitative review of existing literature on aging, productivity, AI and young workers. The analysis distinguishes between augmentative AI, which supports workers in completing tasks, and automative AI, which substitutes for tasks previously performed by labour. The literature suggests that augmentative AI may partially offset aging-related productivity losses by transmitting codified expertise and accelerating learning among less-experienced workers. However, automative AI may reduce entry-level employment and learning-by-doing opportunities. The paper concludes that AI's impact on young workers in aging labour markets depends fundamentally on task allocation and its effects on human-capital formation.

items.title: The Effect of Safety Leadership and Work Pressure on Employee Safety Compliance in the Implementation of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS): A Quantitative Study among Construction Field workers in Bogor
items.abstract: Indonesia’s construction industry continues to face a substantial occupational-safety burden, accounting for approximately 31.9% of reported work-accident cases. This study examines whether safety leadership and work pressure are related to safety compliance among field workers at a construction company in Bogor. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was administered to the entire eligible workforce (n = 37), and the data were analysed using multiple linear regression in SPSS. Safety leadership was positively and significantly related to safety compliance, whereas work pressure did not show a significant partial relationship. Considered jointly, the predictors were significant, although they accounted for a modest proportion of variation in compliance (Adjusted R 2 = 16.1%). These results emphasise the value of supervisors’ visible commitment to safety and indicate that additional factors should be investigated when explaining OHS compliance in construction.

items.title: The Effectiveness of Price Anchors and Second-hand Luxury Products
items.abstract: This study examines the influence of heuristics within the consumption of second-hand luxury items. Prices on second-hand retail platforms were operationalized to test the anchoring heuristic. A mixed-methods design was employed. The quantitative part involved an online experiment utilizing a simulated second-hand luxury purchase scenario to assess the anchoring effect. The qualitative part consisted of semi-structured expert interviews. The data reveal the influence of the anchoring heuristic being attenuated within the luxury sector but significant and in part contingent upon consumers’ per-purchase internal state. The analysis further suggests that price is not the only critical determinant of consumer choice.

items.title: THE EFFICACY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENHANCING WRITING PROFICIENCY AMONG LEARNERS OF CHINESE AS A FOREIGN LANGUAGE
items.abstract: Providing timely, individualized feedback during the writing process remains a persistent Problem of Practice for most language teachers, often leaving learners with delayed support and limited revision opportunities. This mixed-methods crossover study examined whether AI-assisted revision using Claude AI improved Chinese writing performance among high school CFL learners compared with peer revision, whether any advantage transferred to a subsequent unaided writing task, and how learner factors and interactions with AI-generated feedback influenced writing improvement. The study was conducted in a public high school in the eastern United States and involved 40 students in Grades 9–12 enrolled in Chinese 2, Chinese 3, Chinese 4, and AP Chinese courses. Each student completed two five-day writing cycles, revising one essay with AI assistance and one with peer feedback. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, regression, and paired-samples comparisons, while qualitative data from AI interaction logs and survey responses were analyzed using content analysis. Students improved significantly more under AI-assisted revision (M = 1.27 points) than under peer revision (M = 0.13 points; Cohen's d = 1.34), though this advantage did not significantly transfer to a subsequent unaided writing task. Self-rated prompt-writing skill was the only significant predictor of writing improvement. Qualitative findings showed that students most frequently sought AI support for organization, followed by grammar and vocabulary, and perceived AI feedback as helpful while continuing to value teacher feedback. The study highlights prompt literacy as important competency and provides evidence that generative AI can complement, rather than replace, teacher-guided feedback.

items.title: The impact of generative AI application on work efficiency and workload for Generation Z in Jakarta, with AI usage intensity serving as a moderating factor
items.abstract: Despite the fact that generative AI has drastically altered the way Generation Z professionals operate, little research has been done on how it concurrently affects their workload and productivity. We propose that generative AI usage serves as a resource that increases productivity as well as a source of new work demands, and that the intensity of AI usage moderates these impacts. This is based on the Job Demands–Resources theory. We use survey data from 148 Generation Z employees at DKI Jakarta to test our model using PLS-SEM. A productivity paradox is shown by the analysis: the use of generative AI is positively correlated with both work productivity and workload, and the workload impact persists when job demands are the only way to quantify workload. AI usage intensity, the biggest predictor of workload, does not attenuate either connection, suggesting that the demands of generative AI increase with use. By demonstrating that the efficiency gains of generative AI are accompanied by demands that increase with usage, these findings add to the body of research on the adoption of this technology. We talk about the ramifications for businesses looking to use AI without putting too much strain on their employees.

items.title: The New Digital Divide Inside Organizations: AI Access, Career Opportunities and Wage Inequality
items.abstract: Field experiments on generative artificial intelligence (AI) report their largest gains for novices and lower-skilled workers, and this has encouraged a hopeful reading in which the technology narrows skill gaps. Those experiments, however, give access to everybody by design. Inside real organizations, access is allocated by rank, income, occupation and managerial attention. This paper asks who is actually using AI at work, how that use is linked to career opportunities, and what it implies for wage inequality. I combine a structured synthesis of recent experimental, administrative and survey evidence with new calculations on published figures from the Gallup Workforce Panel (more than 30,000 US employees, 2023 to the first quarter of 2026) and Gallup's February 2026 survey of 23,717 employees. Three findings emerge. First, frequent AI use rose in every group, but the gap between leaders and individual contributors grew from 8 to 25 percentage points between 2023 and the second quarter of 2026, even though the ratio between the two stayed near 1.9. Second, frequent use rises by roughly 10 percentage points for each doubling of household income (R² = 0.81 across five income brackets). Third, enabling conditions such as manager support and tool integration are associated with differences of 21 to 34 percentage points in frequent use. A simple break-even calculation shows that the equalizing effect found in experiments disappears once the access ratio between lower- and higher-skilled workers falls to the ratio of their gains per user, and the observed gradients sit close to that threshold under plausible assumptions. Posted wage premiums for AI skills (62 percent on average in 2025) and the fall in early-career hiring in exposed occupations suggest that unequal access can turn into unequal careers. The evidence is descriptive and rests on aggregated secondary data; I set out the limits and a research agenda for linked employer-employee data.

items.title: The Personal PGA Continuity Architecture:
items.abstract: Personal artificial intelligence is often treated as a conversational interface: the user asks, the system answers, and the interaction ends. This white paper proposes a different model. The Personal PGA Continuity Architecture describes a human-centered AI relationship that can adapt not only to the individual, but also to the moment, interface, depth of work, and appropriate return of agency to the human. The framework distinguishes between a mobile or wearable “traveling companion” for immediate capture and clarification and a browser-based deep-work environment for research, analysis, comparison, planning, and document creation. These are presented not as separate intelligences, but as different expressions of one continuing Personal PGA relationship. The paper further explores adaptive depth, pacing, alternative-path exploration, and the Transfer-to-Human Principle (THA), including the idea that returning AI-supported understanding to the human can create space for reflection, reinterpretation, and new human creativity. The central proposition is that meaningful personalization should extend beyond tailored answers to include continuity, modality, pace, depth, alternatives, and preservation of human agency.
